lines.text: Two forces can partly cancel even when each is large. A vector diagram or signed components lets you predict the actual combined force, rather than just adding two positive magnitudes.

A vector has both magnitude and direction. In a plane, i and j are perpendicular unit vectors along the positive horizontal and vertical axes. Write vector v equals x i plus y j with signs showing direction. Its magnitude is the square root of x squared plus y squared, end root. To give its direction, name the reference axis and sense of rotation, then use the component signs to select the quadrant. The resultant of several vectors is their componentwise sum, alternatively, draw the vectors head to tail in a vector diagram. A vector of magnitude V at angle theta above the positive horizontal resolves into open bracket V cosine theta close bracket i plus open bracket V sine theta close bracket j. Prerequisite bridge, recall signed arithmetic, Pythagoras and right triangle trigonometry. Fix the axes before calculating, the modelling assumptions in M1 one point one tell you what object and forces your vector represents.
These same component rules apply to displacements, velocities, accelerations and forces. Once a resultant is known in components, its magnitude and direction describe the combined effect.

Write signed components using i and j. Add like components before finding resultant magnitude. Use the modulus of, x i plus y j, end modulus, equals the square root of x squared plus y squared, end root and check the quadrant for direction. Resolve from the horizontal with V cosine theta horizontally and V sine theta vertically.
Why might the magnitude of the resultant of two forces be smaller than the magnitude of either force?

Find the resultant of three i plus four j and minus five i plus two j. minus two i plus six j eight i plus six j minus two i plus two j two i plus six j ay Add corresponding signed components, three minus five equals minus two and four plus two equals six.
A particle can start away from the origin, or change direction without changing speed. Vector subtraction captures both effects when you calculate motion.

Displacement, velocity, acceleration and force are vectors in a plane, so their horizontal and vertical components carry signs and combine componentwise. For constant velocity, vector v equals open bracket vector r two minus vector r one close bracket over delta t, change in displacement divided by elapsed time. Its magnitude is speed. For constant acceleration, vector a equals open bracket vector v two minus vector v one close bracket over delta t, change in velocity divided by elapsed time. Subtract the entire initial vector, including negative components. Because velocity has direction, speed may stay constant while velocity changes. Forces also add componentwise to give a resultant force. Use m for displacement, metres per second for velocity, metres per second squared for acceleration and N for force. Prerequisite bridge, use M1 two point one to subtract signed components and find a vector magnitude. A time reading is not always the elapsed time, subtract the two readings and retain consistent units.
First resolve or add vectors as in the previous idea. Then divide a change vector by time when the question asks for constant velocity or constant acceleration.

Constant velocity, vector v equals open bracket vector r two minus vector r one close bracket over delta t. Constant acceleration, vector a equals open bracket vector v two minus vector v one close bracket over delta t. Subtract vectors component by component, keeping signs. Speed is velocity magnitude, resultant force is the vector sum of forces.
Why does dividing the final position vector by elapsed time fail when the particle starts away from the origin?

A particle moves from two i minus three j m to eight i plus nine j m in three seconds at constant velocity. Find its velocity. open bracket two i plus four j close bracket metres per second open bracket six i plus twelve j close bracket metres per second open bracket eight i plus nine j close bracket metres per second open bracket two i plus two j close bracket metres per second ay Subtract the first displacement from the second, then divide each component by three seconds.
Find the resultant of three i plus four j and minus five i plus two j.
Add like components, three minus five equals minus two and four plus two equals six. Magnitudes are not added to obtain vector components.
Treat i and j separately.
Keep the negative sign of the second horizontal component.
Add each pair of signed coefficients.
A force of magnitude ten newtons acts thirty degrees above the positive horizontal. Explain how to resolve it into i and j components.
The horizontal side is adjacent to the angle, and the vertical side is opposite it. Both are positive in this quadrant.
Sketch a right triangle with the angle at the horizontal.
Label adjacent and opposite sides.
Apply cosine to the adjacent side and sine to the opposite side.
A force is minus six i plus eight j newtons. Find its magnitude and direction, measured anticlockwise from the positive i direction.

Pythagoras gives the square root of open bracket minus six close bracket squared plus eight squared, end root, equals ten. The vector is in quadrant I I, so the direction is one hundred and eighty degrees minus inverse tangent of open bracket eight over six close bracket is approximately one hundred and twenty six point eight seven degrees.
Locate the quadrant from the component signs.
Use Pythagoras for magnitude.
Find the reference angle, then adjust it for quadrant I I.
Find the constant velocity when displacement changes from two i minus three j metres to eight i plus nine j metres in three seconds.

The displacement change is open bracket eight minus two close bracket i plus open square bracket nine minus open bracket minus three close bracket close square bracket j equals six i plus twelve j metres, dividing by three seconds gives the velocity. Dividing final position alone by time ignores the starting position.
Find the displacement change first.
Subtract the initial vector, including its negative component.
Divide each resulting component by the elapsed time.
Explain why a particle can have non zero acceleration while its speed remains constant.
Constant speed fixes the magnitude of velocity, but the velocity vector may turn, a change in velocity over time is acceleration.
Distinguish speed from velocity.
Consider what happens when direction changes.
Use the definition of acceleration.
A constant force is six i minus eight j newtons and a second constant force is minus two i plus five j newtons. Calculate the resultant force and its magnitude.
Add signed force components to get four i minus three j N. Its magnitude is the square root of four squared plus open bracket minus three close bracket squared, end root, equals five N.
Combine forces as vectors.
Add horizontal and vertical parts separately.
Use Pythagoras on the resultant components.

A displacement is open bracket minus twelve i plus five j close bracket metres, where i points east and j points north. Find part a, its exact magnitude and part b, its three figure bearing, to the nearest degree.

Pythagoras gives the square root of open bracket minus twelve close bracket squared plus five squared, end root, equals thirteen metres. The displacement is west of north by inverse tangent of open bracket twelve over five close bracket is approximately sixty seven point three eight degrees, so its clockwise bearing from north is three hundred and sixty degrees minus sixty seven point three eight degrees is approximately two hundred and ninety three degrees.
Locate the compass quadrant using both component signs.
Use Pythagoras for magnitude and a right triangle for the angle from north.
Bearings are measured clockwise from north, account for the westward component.
A force of magnitude twelve newtons acts at thirty degrees west of north. With i east and j north, find its signed vector components.

The angle is measured from north, so the northward component is twelve cosine thirty degrees equals six the square root of three newtons and the westward component is minus twelve sine thirty degrees equals minus six newtons. The component pair with horizontal magnitude six the square root of three swaps the adjacent and opposite sides, the other incorrect pairs reverse a required compass sign.
Sketch the force arrow and label north and east.
Identify the component adjacent to the angle measured from north.
Use sine for the opposite component, cosine for the adjacent component, then assign compass signs.

A particle moves at constant velocity from position open bracket four i minus seven j close bracket metres to open bracket minus eight i plus nine j close bracket metres in four seconds. Find part a, its complete velocity vector, part b, its speed and part c, its direction, measured anticlockwise from positive i, to the nearest degree.

Subtracting positions gives delta vector r equals open bracket minus twelve i plus sixteen j close bracket metres, hence vector v equals open bracket minus three i plus four j close bracket metres per second and speed five metres per second. The velocity is in quadrant I I, so its direction is one hundred and eighty degrees minus inverse tangent of open bracket four over three close bracket is approximately one hundred and twenty seven degrees anticlockwise from positive i.
Use the change in position rather than the final position alone.
Divide each displacement component by the elapsed time, speed is the resulting vector magnitude.
Subtract initial coordinates with brackets, then use the velocity signs to choose the direction quadrant.

A particle has constant acceleration. Its velocity changes from open bracket minus five i plus seven j close bracket metres per second to open bracket seven i minus two j close bracket metres per second in three seconds. Show that its acceleration is open bracket four i minus three j close bracket metres per second squared, showing the subtraction of each component.

Use vector a equals open bracket vector v minus vector u close bracket over three, the component changes are seven minus open bracket minus five close bracket equals twelve and minus two minus seven equals minus nine. Dividing both by three seconds gives vector a equals open bracket four i minus three j close bracket metres per second squared.
Start from the vector definition of constant acceleration.
Subtract the entire initial velocity vector before dividing by time.
Write each change as final component minus initial component, retaining brackets around negative values.
two Vectors in mechanics.
In one breath.

A vector has magnitude and direction. Write vectors in perpendicular components, combine those components to find a resultant, and use changes in displacement or velocity to calculate velocity or acceleration.
Key ideas.

A scalar has magnitude only, a vector has magnitude and direction. In a horizontal vertical plane, i is a unit vector to the right and j is a unit vector upwards. Thus three i minus four j means three units right and four down. The signs carry the direction, do not discard them while adding vectors.

For vector v equals x i plus y j, its magnitude is the modulus of, vector v, end modulus, equals the square root of x squared plus y squared, end root. Its direction must be stated relative to a named axis, with a sense of rotation. The reference angle satisfies tangent alpha equals the modulus of, y over x, end modulus when x is not equal to zero, but the signs of x and y determine the quadrant. For instance, minus six i plus eight j points into quadrant I I, its direction is about one hundred and twenty seven degrees anticlockwise from positive i, rather than fifty three point one degrees.

To resolve a vector of magnitude V at angle theta above the positive horizontal, use V cosine theta horizontally and V sine theta vertically. The horizontal side is adjacent to the stated angle. If the angle is measured from the vertical, the roles of sine and cosine switch. A vector diagram shows this right triangle and the direction of each component.

The resultant vector is the single vector equivalent to two or more vectors together. Add signed components, open bracket a i plus b j close bracket plus open bracket c i plus d j close bracket equals open bracket a plus c close bracket i plus open bracket b plus d close bracket j. Displacements, velocities, accelerations and forces in a plane all combine by this rule, provided the quantities being added have the same units.
Method.
Choose positive horizontal and vertical directions, and write every vector using i and j.
Resolve angled vectors into signed components. Add components to obtain a resultant, calculate its magnitude only after this addition.

At constant velocity, use vector v equals delta vector r over delta t equals open bracket vector r two minus vector r one close bracket over delta t. The displacement change has units m, and velocity has units metres per second.

At constant acceleration, use vector a equals delta vector v over delta t equals open bracket vector v two minus vector v one close bracket over delta t. Acceleration has units metres per second squared, a change in direction counts as a change in velocity even if speed stays constant.
Head to tail check.

Draw vector a equals four i plus j to scale. From its arrowhead, draw vector b equals minus two i plus three j without changing its length or direction. Draw the resultant from the first arrow's tail to the second arrow's head. Check the net movement, open bracket four minus two close bracket i plus open bracket one plus three close bracket j equals two i plus four j. The resultant's length is the direct start to finish distance, adding the two arrow lengths measures the bent route instead.

Worked example.

A particle moves at constant velocity from two i minus three j m to eight i plus nine j m in three seconds. Find its velocity and speed. First subtract the initial position from the final position, delta vector r equals open bracket eight minus two close bracket i plus open square bracket nine minus open bracket minus three close bracket close square bracket j equals six i plus twelve j metres. Divide by elapsed time, vector v equals open bracket two i plus four j close bracket metres per second. Speed is the magnitude, the modulus of, vector v, end modulus, equals the square root of two squared plus four squared, end root, equals the square root of twenty metres per second is approximately four point four seven metres per second.
Traps.
Trap, Add vector magnitudes to get the resultant magnitude. Why it's wrong, Vectors can oppose or meet at an angle. Instead, Add signed components first, then use Pythagoras.
Trap, Divide the final position by time to find velocity. Why it's wrong, The initial position might not be zero. Instead, Subtract initial position before dividing by elapsed time.
Trap, Use change in speed for acceleration. Why it's wrong, Velocity includes direction. Instead, Subtract the velocity vectors component by component.
Trap, Report only an acute angle. Why it's wrong, It may put the vector in the wrong quadrant. Instead, State the axis, rotation sense and quadrant.
Exam technique.

For Find or Calculate, show the vector equation, the component substitution and the answer with units. If asked to Show that, include every algebraic step leading to the given result. For a force, label components and the resultant in N. For velocity and acceleration, keep the time interval with its unit, round a decimal only at the end. A quick vector diagram can expose a sign error before you calculate.
